entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen9957" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Greeting to Him Who Is Become Known in Righteousness and Salvation</title> <div sID="gen9958" type="x-p"/> This is the only Psalm which is inscribed מזמור without further addition, whence it is called in <hi type="italic">B. Aboda Zara</hi>, 24 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, מזמורא יתומא (the orphan Psalm). The Peshîto Syriac inscribes it <hi type="italic">De redemtione populi ex Aegypto</hi>; the “new song,” however, is not the song of Moses, but the counterpart of this, cf. Rev 15:3. There “the Lord reigneth” resounded for the first time, at the sea; here the completion of the beginning there commenced is sung, viz., the final glory of the divine kingdom, which through judgment breaks through to its full reality. The beginning and end are taken from <reference osisRef="Ps.96.1">Psa 96:1</reference>-13. Almost all that lies between is taken from the second part of Isaiah. This book of consolation for the exiles is become as it were a Castalian spring for the religious lyric.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.98.1-Ps.98.3">Psa 98:1-3</reference> <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.98.1">Psa 98:1</reference></hi> we have already read in Psa 96:1. What follows in <reference osisRef="Ps.98.1">Psa 98:1</reference> is taken from <reference osisRef="Isa.52.10">Isa 52:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.5">Isa 63:5</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.98.7">Psa 98:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.59.16">Psa 59:16</reference>, cf. Psa 40:10. The primary passage, <reference osisRef="Isa.52.10">Isa 52:10</reference>, shows that the <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi> of <reference osisRef="Ps.98.2">Psa 98:2</reference> is correctly placed. לעיני is the opposite of hearsay (cf. Arab. <hi type="italic">l - l - ‛yn</hi>, from one’s own observation, <hi type="italic">opp</hi>. Arab. <hi type="italic">l - l - chbr</hi>, from the narrative of another person). The dative לבית ישראל depends upon ויּזכּר, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.106.45">Psa 106:45</reference>, cf. Luk 1:54.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.98.4-Ps.98.6">Psa 98:4-6</reference> <div eID="gen9958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9959" type="x-p"/> The call in <reference osisRef="Ps.98.4">Psa 98:4</reference> demands some joyful manifestation of the mouth, which can be done in many ways; in <reference osisRef="Ps.98.5">Psa 98:5</reference> the union of song and the music of stringed instruments, as of the Levites; and in <reference osisRef="Ps.98.6">Psa 98:6</reference> the sound of wind instruments, as of the priests. On <reference osisRef="Ps.98.4">Psa 98:4</reference> cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.44.23">Isa 44:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.13">Isa 49:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.52.9">Isa 52:9</reference>, together with <reference osisRef="Isa.14.7">Isa 14:7</reference> (inasmuch as פּצחוּ ורננוּ is equivalent to פּצחוּ רנּה). קול זמרה is found also in Isa 51:3.

On Psa 98:4 cf. Isa 44:23 ; Isa 49:13 ; Isa 52:9 , together with Isa 14:7 (inasmuch as פּצחוּ ורננוּ is equivalent to פּצחוּ רנּה). קול זמרה is found also in Isa 51:3.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.98.7-Ps.98.9">Psa 98:7-9</reference> <div eID="gen9959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9960" type="x-p"/> Here, too, it is all an echo of the earlier language of Psalms and prophets: <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.98.7">Psa 98:7</reference></hi> = <reference osisRef="Ps.96.11">Psa 96:11</reference>; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.98.7">Psa 98:7</reference></hi> like <reference osisRef="Ps.24.1">Psa 24:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.98.8">Psa 98:8</reference> after <reference osisRef="Isa.55.12">Isa 55:12</reference> (where we find מחא כּף instead of the otherwise customary תּקע כּף, <reference osisRef="Ps.47.2">Psa 47:2</reference>; or הכּה כּף, 2Ki 11:12, is said of the trees of the field); <reference osisRef="Ps.98.9">Psa 98:9</reference> - <reference osisRef="Ps.96.13">Psa 96:13</reference>, cf. Psa 36:10. In the bringing in of nature to participate in the joy of mankind, the clapping rivers (נהרות) are original to this Psalm: the rivers cast up high waves, which flow into one another like clapping hands;<note placement="foot">Luther renders: “the water-floods exult” (<hi type="italic">frohlocken</hi>); and <hi type="italic">Eychman’s Vocabularius</hi> predicantium explains <hi type="italic">plaudere</hi> by “to exult (<hi type="italic">frohlocken</hi>) for joy, to smite the hands together <hi type="italic">prae gaudio</hi>;” cf. Luther’s version of Eze 21:17.</note> cf. <reference osisRef="Hab.3.10">Hab 3:10</reference>, where the abyss of the sea lifts up its hands on high, i.e., causes its waves to run mountain-high.  <chapter eID="Ps.98"/> <div eID="gen9960" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: Psa 98:7-9 Here, too, it is all an echo of the earlier language of Psalms and prophets: Psa 98:7 = Psa 96:11 ; Psa 98:7 like Psa 24:1 ; Psa 98:8 after Isa 55:12 (where we find מחא כּף instead of the otherwise customary תּקע כּף, Psa 47:2 ; or הכּה כּף, 2Ki 11:12, is said of the trees of the field); Psa 98:9 - Psa 96:13 , cf. Psa 36:10. In the bringing in of nature to participate in the joy of mankind, the clapping rivers (נהרות) are original to this Psalm: the rivers cast up high waves, which flow into one another like clapping hands; Luther renders: “the water-floods exult” ( frohlocken ); and Eychman’s Vocabularius predicantium explains plaudere by “to exult ( frohlocken ) for joy, to smite the hands together prae gaudio ;” cf. Luther’s version of Eze 21:17. cf. Hab 3:10 , where the abyss of the sea lifts up its hands on high, i.e., causes its waves to run mountain-high.
